do-i-need-to-hire-another-employee.html.text:
← Shift roster builder

Do I need to hire another employee? Test the schedule first

"We are short-staffed" can mean three different things: not enough hours in the team, not enough people at the times you need them, or one person everything depends on. Only the first is fixed by adding a person at random. Checking takes a few minutes, before you spend money on a job post.

Open the free roster builder

Step 1: hours needed against hours available

Multiply each shift's length by the people it needs and add up the week. Then add every person's weekly hour limit. If the first number is larger, no schedule can cover the week, whatever the arrangement. The builder prints this warning for you when it happens.

A worked example: a four-person salon

The numbers below are invented and were produced by the builder itself; the page's tests re-run them, so they cannot drift from the tool.

PersonWageWeekly limitAvailable
Maya$2440 hTue–Sat 9–19
Jo$2036 hMon–Fri 9–19
Priya$1824 hThu–Sun 10–20
Sam$1520 hMon–Sat 9–19

The shop needs two people 9–2 and two people 2–7 on weekdays, three people 10–6 on Saturday and one person 10–4 on Sunday: 130 hours a week. The team's limits add up to 120 hours, so the answer to step 1 is already "no, not as it stands".

Step 2: see where it breaks

The builder fills 97 of the 130 hours and leaves 6 shifts open (33 hours): two Monday afternoon places, Tuesday, Wednesday and Friday afternoons, and one Saturday place. For each one it says why. Monday afternoon, for example: two people are free, but one would break the 10-hour rest rule and one is at their weekly limit. Sunday is only coverable by Priya, so if she is sick the shop is closed.

Step 3: test the hire before you make it

Adding a person to the list costs nothing. With one extra part-timer at $17 an hour, up to 30 hours, free any time, the week goes from 6 open shifts to 1 open shift (5 hours). The new person works 28 hours and total payroll rises from $1,904 to $2,380. The builder's own "what if we hired" test, which assumes an average wage of $19.25 and 40 hours, gives the same picture: 28 hours covered, 5 still open, about $545 more payroll a week. That is the price of those 28 hours, and the figure to compare with what the uncovered chairs would earn.

Two things to read off that result. The remaining gap is a Monday afternoon place: Maya and Priya do not work Mondays, so only Jo, Sam and the new person can. That suggests asking for Monday availability in the job post, not just hours. And it shows who the week depends on: with Maya out, 28 more hours go uncovered, more than anyone else.

Try it with your own team

Questions

How do I know if I need to hire another employee?

Add up the hours your shifts require and compare them with the combined weekly hour limits of your current team. If the shifts need more than the team can give, hiring or cutting shifts is unavoidable. If the team has enough hours on paper but shifts still go uncovered, the problem is availability, not headcount, and a person with wider availability fixes it better than more hours do.

Is it cheaper to pay overtime or hire a part-timer?

Overtime hours cost a premium, often time and a half, on top of the wage. A part-timer costs the wage but also carries hiring, training and payroll-tax costs. For a few short weeks overtime is usually cheaper; for a gap that repeats every week, a hire is. Test both by running the schedule with and without the extra person.

Does the tool say whether my schedule is legal?

No. It applies the rest, hour and overtime rules you type in. It does not know your local scheduling-notice, break or minor-labor laws.

No warranty. Free and as-is, without warranty of any kind. This page is general information, not legal, tax or financial advice, and it does not tell you what scheduling law requires of you. Rules vary by place and change; check current guidance or ask a qualified professional. The example is invented.

Everything the roster builder does runs in your browser; your staff list is never uploaded. Free and open source: support is entirely optional. Related: how to make an employee schedule, the shift-cover optimizer.

How to fill in the template by hand

What should an employee schedule template include?

The week's start date, a row per person, a column per day with start and end times, each person's total hours, and a note of who is on call or unavailable. Print it, fill it in, and post it where staff can see it.

How do I fill in a weekly schedule template?

List the shifts the business must cover each day, then place people whose availability fits, starting with the people who have the fewest options. Check each person's total against their hour limit and look for a late close followed by an early open.

free-alternative-to-7shifts-when-i-work-.text:
← Shift roster builder

A free alternative to 7shifts, When I Work, Homebase and Deputy for building the rota

Scheduling apps bundle several jobs: building the week, telling staff, trading shifts, clocking in and paying. If what hurts on Sunday night is the first one, you do not need all of them. This page says plainly which part the free roster builder covers and which it does not.

Open the free roster builder

Which job do you need done?

The jobWhere to do it
Fill a week of shifts from staff availability, hour limits and wages, with no one in overtime who need not beThis tool. Paste or upload the staff list, get a roster, a list of shifts nobody could take and why, and who the week depends on.
Tell staff their shiftsThis tool: a calendar file per person, a text to paste, and an optional self-hosted team page (below).
Staff swap shifts and ask for time offThe self-hosted team page handles requests and the manager approves; swaps are checked against rest and hour rules.
Clock in and out, geofencing, payroll exportA scheduling suite. This tool has none of it.
Push notifications and a mobile staff appA scheduling suite. The team page is a web link, not a notifying app.
Integrations with your point-of-sale or payrollA scheduling suite. This tool exports CSV and calendar files only.

What this tool does differently

It runs in your browser, so your staff list and their wages are never uploaded and nobody makes an account. It treats availability, rest gaps, weekly and daily limits, minors' hours, split-shift premiums and overtime as rules, searches for the cheapest roster that covers the most hours, and tells you before the week starts which shifts cannot be filled and what blocks each one. The source is MIT-licensed, so a small team can also run its own copy of the team page without a per-user price.

Try it without typing: pick a template (cafe, salon, shop, clinic) and it builds a roster for an invented team straight away.

Try it with your own team

Where it falls short

  • It is a heuristic search, not a proof of the cheapest possible roster on large problems.
  • It does not know local predictive-scheduling, break or minor-labor law; you enter the rules that apply to you.
  • The self-hosted team page has no accounts and no automatic notifications.
  • We make no claim about any paid product's features, accuracy or current prices, and have not evaluated them; check their own sites. Choose by which jobs in the table above you actually need.

Questions

Is there a free alternative to 7shifts, When I Work, Homebase or Deputy?

For the rota-building part, yes: the free roster builder fills as many shifts as your rules allow, names the ones nobody can take, and runs in your browser with no account. It does not replace time clocks, payroll, push notifications or a staff app. Teams that need those still need a scheduling suite.

Can I run my own team schedule without paying per user?

Yes. The roster builder repository includes a small self-hosted server: you publish the week, your team opens one link to see their shifts and add them to a calendar, and it sends you their availability and shift-trade requests. It is MIT-licensed, has no dependencies and runs on a disk you own.

What does the roster builder do that a spreadsheet does not?

It checks availability, rest gaps, hour limits and overtime for you, searches for the cheapest roster that still covers the most shift-hours, and tells you which shifts cannot be filled and why before the week starts.

how-to-avoid-clopening.html.text:
← Shift roster builder

How to avoid clopening: what a rest gap between shifts costs

A clopening is a late close followed by an early open: someone locks up at 11pm and unlocks at 6am. The standard fix is a minimum rest gap between any two of a person's shifts. Owners worry that a rule like that leaves shifts empty or raises payroll. We measured it.

Open the free roster builder

The experiment

The roster builder's built-in invented example: a seven-person cafe, 32 shifts, 235 hours to cover, a 40-hour overtime line, and each person's own availability. Only the rest gap changed between runs; everything else is the tool's defaults.

Minimum rest gapShifts left openHours coveredPayroll
None (0 h)2219 of 235$3,671
8 h3216$3,620
10 h3216$3,622
12 h3216$3,630
14 h5215$3,611

What it shows

For this cafe, a rest gap anywhere from 8 to 12 hours left one more shift open than no rule (3 against 2, three fewer hours covered) and cut payroll by roughly $40 to $50 because that last awkward shift went unstaffed rather than paid for. The search gave the other close-then-open pairs to different people. At 14 hours the rule starts to bite: two more shifts go open. So the question to ask of your own week is where your cliff is, not whether a rule is affordable in general. This is one invented example, not a benchmark, and your availability decides your numbers.

Find the cliff in your own week

How to do it by hand

1. Mark every close and every open

List who works each closing shift, then check the next morning's opens for the same names.

2. Swap one side of each pair

Move either the close or the open to someone who is free and not already near their weekly limit. Do the people with the narrowest availability first.

3. Watch the week boundary

Sunday night's close and Monday morning's open are the pair most often missed. The roster builder can read last week's roster CSV so the rule holds across Monday.

Questions

What does clopening mean in scheduling?

It means working a closing shift and then the opening shift the next morning, leaving little time to sleep. A minimum rest gap between shifts is the usual way to prevent it.

How many hours of rest should be between shifts?

There is no single answer. Some employers use 8 to 12 hours as policy and some places regulate it for certain workers. Check the rules where you operate. The roster builder lets you set the gap and will not break it.

how-to-cover-a-shift-when-someone-calls-.text:
← Shift roster builder

How to cover a shift when someone calls out: patch it or rebuild the week

Somebody texts at 6am that they are not coming in. You have two moves: patch (give that one shift to someone else and touch nothing more) or rebuild (mark the person off and re-plan the week, which can move other people's shifts). Which one works depends mostly on how full the week already was. We measured it.

Open the free roster builder

The experiment

The roster builder's built-in invented example: a seven-person cafe, 32 shifts, 235 hours to cover, a 40-hour overtime line and a 10-hour rest gap. We took every person-day on the finished roster (each is one possible call-out) and tried both moves, with the rest of the week fixed. Then we added one spare part-timer (15 an hour, up to 24 hours, free any time) and ran it again. “Covered” means the move created no new open hours.

StaffPossible call-outsPatched with one swapRebuild covers itShifts a rebuild moves
The cafe as given290132 to 19
Plus one spare part-timer3211813 to 24

What it shows

A one-for-one swap almost never works on a week that was built to use everyone: the people who are free that hour are already at their weekly limit, on another shift, or inside their rest gap. A rebuild finds a cover far more often, but it is not free. It re-plans the whole week, so it moved between 2 and 24 shifts, which is a lot of text messages. A spare part-timer lifts the rebuilds that find cover from 13 of 29 to 18 of 32, but it makes each rebuild move more people. The practical lesson is to decide in advance who your first call is, and to treat a rebuild as a last resort once the swap list comes back empty. This is one invented example, not a benchmark, and your own availability decides your numbers.

Test a call-out on your own week

How to do it by hand

1. List who could take the shift

Write down everyone whose availability covers the whole shift, who is not already working then, and who still has hours under their weekly limit.

2. Check rest and overtime

Cross out anyone who would then work less than your minimum rest gap before or after, and price anyone who would go into overtime against leaving the shift one person short.

3. If the list is empty, look for a two-step swap

Ask whether a person who cannot take the shift can give up a lighter shift to someone who can. The roster builder lists these trades.

Questions

What do you do when an employee calls out?

Find who is free, under their hour limit and rested enough to take the shift. If nobody is, rebuild the week with the absent person marked off, which can move other people's shifts. The roster builder does both: the sick-call finder lists who can take a shift, and an off: entry rebuilds around the absence.

How do you cover a shift at the last minute?

Ask the people whose availability and weekly hours leave room first, since they cost no overtime. If the shift is thin rather than empty, leaving it short for one day is sometimes cheaper than paying overtime. Check the rules where you operate before asking anyone to work extra.

how-to-handle-time-off-requests.html.text:
← Shift roster builder

How many time-off requests can you grant before a shift goes empty?

Every request looks fine on its own. The trouble is the fourth one, when the people who were covering for the first three are now the ones asking. A good rule is to grant requests one at a time and rebuild the week after each, so you find the request that tips a shift into empty before you have promised it. We measured where that happens for one cafe.

Open the free roster builder

The experiment

The roster builder's built-in invented example: a seven-person cafe, 32 shifts, 235 hours to cover, a 40-hour overtime line and a 10-hour rest gap. We granted a Saturday-and-Sunday request to the five people with the widest weekend availability, one at a time in the order shown, and rebuilt the week after each. Everything else is the tool's defaults.

Weekends off granted toShifts left openHours covered of 235Payroll
Nobody3216$3,622
Ana3216$3,624
Ana, Gus4213$3,561
Ana, Gus, Dev5200$3,337
Ana, Gus, Dev, Cleo7182$3,067
Ana, Gus, Dev, Cleo, Eli9169$2,906

What it shows

The first request is nearly free: the week still covers 216 hours and payroll moves by $2. The second costs a shift. By the fifth, more than a quarter of the week's hours are uncovered, and the payroll that "fell" is only the pay for shifts nobody is working. So the number to watch is open shifts, not cost. This is one invented example, not a benchmark, and your availability decides where your limit falls.

Try your own requests

How to do it by hand

1. Rank requests by how few people could cover

For each requested day, count the people who are available for the busiest shift and are not also asking. Grant the requests with the most spare cover first.

2. Recheck after every approval

Each yes uses up someone who could have covered the next one, so the count drops by more than one.

3. Say no early, with a reason

Tell a person which shift would go empty. People take a specific reason better than silence. Check the rules where you operate for any notice or approval rules that apply.

Questions

How many time-off requests can I approve at once?

There is no fixed number; it depends on how many other people are available when the requester is off. Grant them one at a time and rebuild the week after each: the first request that leaves a shift open is the limit for that week. The roster builder takes an off: entry per person and shows any shift it can no longer fill.

How do I schedule around time-off requests?

Put the approved days off into each person's availability before you assign anyone, so the schedule never gives them a shift on those days, then check whether any shift went uncovered. The roster builder reads an off: entry, such as off: Sat-Sun, and re-plans the week around it.

how-to-make-an-employee-schedule.html.text:
← Shift roster builder

How to make an employee schedule that covers every shift

Most small-business schedules are made on Sunday night from memory, a spreadsheet and a few text messages. The same four things go wrong: a shift nobody noticed was uncovered, someone scheduled on a day they cannot work, an avoidable overtime week, and the same two people getting all the good (or all the bad) shifts. Doing the steps in the right order fixes most of it.

Open the free roster builder

The method

1. Write the shifts down as requirements, not as names

For each day: start, end, how many people it takes. "Mon–Fri 6–2, two people, open" is a requirement; "Ana and Ben on opens" is already a decision. Keeping them apart is what lets you see the real total of hours you must cover.

2. Write down each person's hard limits

Availability windows, the most hours they can or want to work, and the fewest you have promised. Days not on the list count as unavailable. If the weekly limits of everyone together are smaller than the hours to cover, no schedule works and it is better to learn that before the week starts.

3. Apply the hard rules before you think about money

A person must be free for the whole shift, cannot be in two places, needs enough rest since their last shift, and has a cap on days in a row. These are not preferences. The most constrained shifts (the ones only one or two people can work) go first, or the easy shifts will use up exactly the people the hard ones need.

4. Then trade cost, overtime and fairness

Among the schedules that obey the rules, an overtime hour costs a premium, so keep people under the threshold when someone else is free. Giving every hour to the cheapest person is cheap on paper and loses staff, so a fair share of hours and a minimum for the people you have promised them belong in the score too.

5. Look for the single points of failure

Remove each person in turn and see which shifts go uncovered. Anyone whose absence leaves a shift open is who the week depends on: they need a backup, or a wider availability from someone else.

A worked example

An invented café has seven people and 32 shifts to fill across the week, 235 hours in all, with a 10-hour rest rule, a 40-hour overtime line and everyone's own availability. Filling shifts in time order with the first free name on the list leaves 7 shifts open, 58 hours nobody is scheduled for. The roster builder, given the same people and rules, leaves 3 shifts open and tells you why for each: for example the Monday lunch has four people free, but all four are already at their weekly limit. It also reports that taking out any one of Ana, Dev or Gus leaves 40 more hours uncovered, so those three are the café's single points of failure. The fix is a decision for the owner: ask Fay or Cleo for wider availability, add an hour limit exception, or shorten a shift.

Try it with your own week

Questions

What is a clopening and why do schedules avoid it?

A clopening is a closing shift followed by an opening shift the next morning, leaving very little time to sleep. Some places limit it by law or policy with a minimum rest gap between shifts, often somewhere around 8 to 11 hours. Check what applies where you operate; the roster builder lets you set the gap and will not break it.

How do I avoid overtime when making a schedule?

Count each person's hours across the whole pay week, not shift by shift, and give the marginal shift to someone who is still under the threshold even if they cost slightly more per hour. One overtime hour at time and a half costs more than an extra hour for anyone paid up to half as much again as the person already at the limit.

How far in advance do I have to post a schedule?

It depends on where you operate. Some cities and states have predictive-scheduling or fair-workweek rules with advance-notice periods and pay for late changes, usually aimed at larger retail, food-service and hospitality employers. This tool does not check them, so look up the rules for your location.

how-to-reduce-overtime-in-a-schedule.htm.text:
← Shift roster builder

How to reduce overtime in a weekly schedule: what the overtime line costs

Overtime is rarely planned. It happens when the same few people are the only ones free for the long shifts, and the schedule is built one shift at a time. The fix is to count hours as you assign and, where you can, hand the shift to someone still under the line. We measured how much overtime one invented week still needs, and what it costs, at three different lines.

Open the free roster builder

The experiment

The roster builder's built-in invented example: a seven-person cafe, 32 shifts, 235 hours to cover, each person's own availability and weekly hour limit, a 10-hour rest gap. Only the overtime line changed between runs (hours past the line are paid at 1.5 times the wage); everything else is the tool's defaults.

Overtime lineOvertime hours in the best rosterHours coveredPayroll
30 h30216 of 235$3,890
35 h13216$3,739
40 h0216$3,622

What it shows

At a 40-hour line this cafe can be covered with no overtime at all. Moving the line to 35 hours, the same schedule can no longer avoid 13 hours of premium pay, and at 30 hours it is 30 hours, about $270 more a week than at 40. Coverage did not change in any run: the search protected covered hours first and let the premium fall where it was cheapest. So the useful question about your own week is how many hours sit just past your line, and who could take them. This is one invented example, not a benchmark, and your availability decides your numbers.

See the overtime in your own week

How to do it by hand

1. Keep a running total per person

Write each person's hours beside their name and update it after every shift you assign.

2. Fill the hardest shifts first

Give the shifts few people can work to those people early, while they have room, then fill the easy shifts around them.

3. Split the last long shift

If the only person free would cross the line, cut the shift into two shorter ones for two people instead. The roster builder does this when it is cheaper.

Questions

How do you reduce overtime when making a schedule?

Count each person's hours as you assign shifts and give the next shift to someone who is free and still under the overtime line. When everyone available is near the line, split the long shift or hire cover. The roster builder prices overtime into its search, so it gives hours to people under the line before it pays a premium.

When does overtime start?

It depends on where you operate and who the worker is. Many places count hours over 40 in a week, and some also count hours over a daily limit. Check the rules that apply to you. The roster builder lets you enter your own weekly and daily lines.

how-to-rotate-closing-and-weekend-shifts.text:
← Shift roster builder

How to rotate closing and weekend shifts fairly

Closes, early opens and weekends are the shifts people trade favours over. When the same two or three people keep getting them, they quit or stop covering for others. The fix is to count the tough shifts and hand the next one to whoever has the fewest. Doing that by hand for six people over two months is tedious; a roster search can do it while it fills the week. We measured how much it helps.

Open the free roster builder

The experiment

An invented six-person team, all on $15 an hour and available any time, up to 40 hours each, and the roster builder's example cafe shifts (open, lunch and close on weekdays, Saturday and Sunday). That is 8 weeks of plans, each carrying the last week's tally forward. A "tough" shift is a weekend shift, a close at 10pm or later, or an open at 6am or earlier. Only the Spread weekend, closing and opening shifts setting changed.

Spread settingMost tough shifts (one person)FewestGapEight-week payrollOpen hours
0 (off)40328$28,2000
1037352$28,2000
3037343$28,2000

What it shows

With the setting off, one person closed or worked weekends 40 times in eight weeks and another 32: eight extra tough shifts, a full extra week of them. A small setting of 10 narrowed that to two, with no extra payroll and no shift left open, because here everyone costs the same and can work any time. Turning it up to 30 did not help further; the first step does the work. Real teams are lumpier: if only two people can close, no setting can rotate to a third. In the builder's own example cafe, availability alone decides who closes and the setting changes nothing, which is itself worth knowing before you argue about fairness. These are invented numbers, not a benchmark.

Check the spread on your own team

How to do it by hand

1. Keep one tally

Per person, count weekend shifts, closes and early opens worked in the last month. One column in a spreadsheet is enough.

2. Fill the hardest shifts first

Assign the closes and weekends before the easy middle shifts, and give each to the person with the lowest tally who is free.

3. Carry it across weeks

A fresh start each Monday resets the count and favours whoever is easiest to schedule. In the roster builder, "Carry over last week" fills each person's tally from the roster CSV you posted, fading older weeks, and "Plan several weeks" shows the totals per person.

Questions

How do you rotate closing shifts fairly?

Count each person's closing, opening and weekend shifts over several weeks, then give the next tough shift to whoever has the fewest. In the roster builder, raise the spread setting and the search does that for you without leaving any shift open.

Does a fair rotation cost more payroll?

Not when staff have the same wage and availability: in the example on this page the eight-week payroll was identical with and without the rotation setting. When wages differ, the setting can shift hours toward costlier people, so check the payroll line.

index.html.text:
SHIFT ROSTER BUILDER · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

Build this week's schedule without the spreadsheet puzzle

List the shifts you need covered and your people with their availability, weekly hour limits and wages. The tool assigns people to shifts so that every shift is covered if it can be, nobody works outside their availability, gets less rest than you allow, or goes into overtime when someone cheaper is free. Shifts it cannot fill come back with the reason, and it shows who the week depends on. Download the roster as a CSV.

Your staff list never leaves this browser tab. Planning aid, not legal, tax, or financial advice. It does not know your local scheduling-notice, break or minor-labor laws. See how to make an employee schedule for the method, and do I need to hire another employee? for testing a hire before you post the job. Checking payroll against sales? See labor cost percentage by day. Worried about close-then-open shifts? See what a rest gap costs, or how to reduce overtime in a schedule. Scheduling a 14 or 15 year old? See what the youth hour limits do to a roster, a free alternative to paid scheduling apps for the rota. Need a blank grid to print? See the free weekly employee schedule template. Closes and weekends landing on the same people? See how to rotate them fairly. Someone just called out? See patch it or rebuild the week. Weekend requests piling up? See how many you can grant. Shifts staying open? See whose availability is worth asking to widen.

Your people

Availability is days and hours separated by semicolons: Mon-Fri 9-17; Sat 10am-2pm; Sun off. Days you do not list count as unavailable; leave it blank or write any for always free. Max hours default to 40.

Shifts to cover

Days can be a range (Mon-Fri) or a list (Mon/Wed/Fri). Times can be 9, 9:30 or 9am. An end at or before the start runs overnight into the next day. People needed makes that many separate shifts. To lock a shift to someone, add fixed: Ana as a last cell (use fixed: Ana + Ben to pin two copies); the tool plans everyone else around it.

Each week starts from the one before: rest gaps and who closed lately carry over, and dated off: days land in their own week. Uses the settings above and the Monday in "Week starting".
The link holds the whole setup, wages included, in the part after # that no server receives. Send it only to people who may see pay.

Sets each person's prev: (when their last shift ended) so rest rules hold across Monday.

Your people, shifts and settings are remembered on this device only (browser local storage), so next week you can open the page and click the button.

Enter your people and shifts, then click the button.

Collect your team's availability

Stop chasing availability in group chats. Make a link, send it to your team, and each person fills a week grid and sends you one line back. Paste the lines below and they replace each person's availability in your staff list; wages, roles and the hours cap you set stay (a person can only lower their own max hours). The link carries only the business name, week and, if you add it, one person's name; nothing is stored or uploaded.

Result

The roster

Hours and pay by person

PersonShiftsHoursOvertimePayrollAgainst their limits

Who this week depends on

Re-builds the week without each person. If shifts then go uncovered, that person is a single point of failure.

Changes since you posted it

Posted a schedule, then changed it? Choose the roster CSV you posted, say when you made the change, and see every shift that was added, cancelled or moved, how much notice each got, and the premium pay your own rule would owe. Fair-workweek laws differ by city and change: enter your window and premium from the rule that applies to you; nothing here is a statement of what a law requires.

Someone called in sick? Who can take the shift

Pick a shift. It lists everyone who could take it without touching anyone else's week, cheapest first, and why the rest cannot.

Two people want to swap? Check the trade

Pick the two shifts they hold. It says whether trading them keeps both weeks inside every rule, what it does to payroll, and which rule stops it if not.

Someone out for several days? Re-cover all their shifts

Pick the person and the days they are out. Every shift they hold on those days goes to someone else, cheapest first, without moving anyone else's existing shifts. Shifts nobody can take stay open, with the reason.

Days out (none ticked = the whole week)

Against filling shifts in listed order

What you get by going through the shifts in time order and giving each to the first person in your list who is free and within the rules.

PlanShifts left openOvertime hoursPayroll
No pay or wages on it, so it is safe to post in the break room.

How it is calculated

Hard rules (never broken): a person is only given a shift that falls inside one of their availability windows for the whole shift; shifts for one person never overlap and leave at least your rest gap between them; weekly hours stay at or under their maximum; days in a row stay at or under your limit. Objective: first cover as many shift-hours as possible, then minimise real payroll (wage × (1 + extras), overtime hours above your threshold at the multiplier), plus a small penalty for each hour a person is under their minimum and a quadratic penalty for hours drifting from a fair share (the balance slider). Search: a greedy build that fills the most constrained shifts first, then seeded simulated annealing with reassign and swap moves over several restarts; a fixed seed makes it repeatable. On small problems the tests compare it with an exhaustive search of every roster and it finds the same optimum; on large ones it is a strong heuristic, not a proof.

Not modelled: predictive-scheduling and fair-workweek rules as built-in law (the page flags a short-notice week and a changes report prices a premium you enter), paid rest breaks (unpaid meal breaks are deducted and suggested break times are shown, but breaks are not a hard rule), minor-labor limits beyond a per-person daily: cap, union rules, seniority, time off requests across weeks (a running tough: 3 cell, filled in by “carry over last week”, remembers who closed or worked weekends lately so the next week spreads them fairly when the spread setting is above 0; one week's time off works: add off: Wed; Fri 5pm-close to a person; a soft wish works too: prefer: Sat gives that person those hours when it costs nothing; avoid: Sat; Fri 5pm-close keeps those hours free unless the roster would otherwise leave a shift open or cost more). The rest rule does carry over from last week if you add prev: Sun 10pm to a person (when their last shift ended). Roles work: role: keyholder x1 on a shift needing 3 people asks for one keyholder among them. Unverified: checked against exhaustive search and invented data in unit tests, not against a real operator's payroll or a scheduling law.

Common questions

How do I make an employee schedule that covers every shift?

List each shift you need covered with how many people it takes, list each person with their availability, weekly hour limits and wage, and assign people to shifts one hard rule at a time: available for the whole shift, not double-booked, enough rest since their last shift, under their weekly limit. This tool does that search for you and shows any shift it could not fill with the reason.

How does the roster builder decide who works which shift?

It never breaks a hard rule (availability, weekly hour cap, rest between shifts, consecutive days, no double-booking). Among the rosters that follow those rules it covers as many shifts as possible first, then picks the lowest payroll, counting overtime above your threshold, nudged by the hour balance slider and by each person's minimum hours. The search is a seeded simulated-annealing optimiser, so the same inputs always give the same roster.

Is the roster guaranteed to be the cheapest possible?

No. Choosing who works which shift is a hard combinatorial problem, so the tool searches rather than proves optimality. On small problems the test suite checks the result against an exhaustive search of every possible roster and it matches. On a full week it finds a strong roster quickly, and the result is deterministic so you can compare changes fairly.

What does the hour balance slider do?

At zero the tool chases the lowest payroll, which can pile hours on the cheapest people and leave others under their minimum. Raising it adds a penalty for each person's hours drifting from their fair share of the total, in proportion to their weekly limit. Payroll shown is always the real cost, not the penalised score.

What does who-is-critical mean?

For each person on the roster the tool re-builds the week without them and reports how many hours of shifts would then go uncovered. A person whose absence leaves hours uncovered is a single point of failure: one sick call and a shift is open. Use it to see where you need a backup or wider availability.

What rules and laws does it check?

It enforces the availability, weekly hour limit, rest gap and consecutive-day limit that you type in, and prices weekly overtime above the threshold you set, plus optional daily overtime and double time (California-style presets included). It does not know your local predictive-scheduling or fair-workweek notice rules, break and meal-period rules, minor-labor limits, union terms or tip rules, which vary by place. Check the roster against the rules that apply to you.

Is my staff list uploaded anywhere?

No. Names, wages and availability are read and solved in this browser tab. Nothing is sent to a server, there are no accounts or cookies, and the tool does not store your roster. It works offline once the page has loaded.

It is not legal, tax, or financial advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional or your own knowledge of the labor rules that apply to you. labor-cost-percentage-by-day.html.text:
← Shift roster builder

Labor cost percentage: how to calculate it, by week and by day

Labor cost percentage is payroll divided by sales for the same period. The formula is easy. The useful part is doing it for each day of the schedule you are about to post, because the weekly number averages away the days that lose money.

Open the free roster builder

The formula

Labor % = scheduled payroll ÷ projected sales × 100. Scheduled payroll is hours times each person's wage, plus any overtime premium, plus payroll taxes and benefits if you want the full cost. Projected sales is your forecast for the same days, usually last year's or last month's matching week.

A worked example

An invented café has seven people. The roster builder schedules 216 hours for a payroll of $3,622, and three shifts stay open. Two possible weeks:

Projected weekly salesLabor %Against a 30% target
$14,00025.9%$578 under the $4,200 limit
$12,00030.2%$22 over the $3,600 limit

Now enter daily sales of $1,500, $1,600, $1,700, $1,900, $2,600, $3,200 and $2,400 (Monday to Sunday):

DayHoursPayrollSalesLabor %
Mon32$548$1,50036.5%
Tue35$604$1,60037.8%
Wed35$594$1,70034.9%
Thu35$604$1,90031.8%
Fri27$470$2,60018.1%
Sat28$434$3,20013.6%
Sun24$368$2,40015.3%

Tuesday is the worst day at 37.8%, and the weekend runs at about half that. The week as a whole looks acceptable, but staffing is thickest on the quietest days. Moving hours from the early week to Friday and Saturday, within each person's availability and limits, is a decision the daily view makes visible. Daily payroll excludes the overtime premium, which is priced weekly.

Try it with your own week

Questions

What is a good labor cost percentage?

There is no single right number. It depends on the kind of business, how much of your service is labor versus product, and your prices. Compare against your own past weeks first; published industry ranges differ by source and should be treated as a rough check, not a target.

Should labor cost include payroll taxes and benefits?

Usually yes if you want the true cost of a shift. Wages alone understate it. The roster builder lets you add a burden percentage on top of wages; use the rate your accountant gives you.

Why look at labor percentage by day instead of by week?

A week can sit under target while the quiet days run far over it and the busy days run far under. The daily view shows which shifts to trim and where an extra person pays for themselves.

scheduling-14-and-15-year-olds.html.text:
← Shift roster builder

Scheduling 14 and 15 year olds: what the hour limits do to a roster

Teenagers are cheap, keen and available after school, which is why cafes, shops and salons hire them. They are also the staff whose hours the law limits most tightly, and the limits quietly change which shifts they can take at all. We measured it.

Open the free roster builder

The US federal limits

For 14 and 15 year olds the federal rules are: work only between 7am and 7pm (9pm from June 1 to Labor Day); in a school week at most 3 hours on a school day and 18 hours; outside school at most 8 hours a day and 40 hours a week. States add work permits, break rules and tighter hours, and the stricter rule wins, so treat this as a floor.

The experiment

The roster builder's invented seven-person cafe: 32 shifts, 235 hours to cover. Cleo and Eli are the two youngest on the team. Only their ages changed between runs, using the age: cell; everything else is the tool's defaults.

Cleo and EliShifts left openHours coveredPayrollCleo + Eli hours
No age set3216$3,62236
Cleo 15, school weeks5200$3,38218
Cleo 15 and Eli 14, school weeks8176$3,0190
Both, summer4208$3,48332

What it shows

In a school week neither teenager fits a single shift. The cafe's shifts run 6 to 14 and 14 to 22 and the limits stop work at 7pm and cap a day at 3 hours, so a whole 8-hour shift never fits inside what they may do. The two of them go from 36 hours to none and five more shifts go unfilled; the payroll falls only because the hours disappear. In summer the window widens to 9pm and the day to 8 hours, and most of it comes back. The lesson is not that teenagers are a bad hire. It is that a teenager needs short shifts built for them (a 3-hour 4pm to 7pm slot, or a weekend half-day) rather than a place in the adult rota.

This is one invented example, not a benchmark. The page applies the 3-hour school-day cap to every day in school mode, which is the cautious reading; the federal rule counts only school days, so for Saturdays use the summer setting or an off: cell for school hours.

Try it with your own team

How to do it by hand

1. Write down each teenager's window

Start from the legal window (7am to 7pm in term), then take away school hours and anything their parents have told you.

2. Carve short shifts out of the busy periods

The after-school rush and weekend lunch are where a 3-hour shift helps most. Add them as separate shifts instead of trimming an adult shift.

3. Never leave them alone

Put an adult on every stretch a minor works. The roster builder flags any stretch where only people marked as minors are on shift.

Questions

What are the federal hour limits for 14 and 15 year olds?

Under the US Fair Labor Standards Act, 14 and 15 year olds may work only between 7am and 7pm (9pm from June 1 to Labor Day), for at most 3 hours on a school day, 18 hours in a school week, 8 hours on a non-school day and 40 hours in a non-school week. Many states are stricter and some require work permits, so check yours.

How do I enter a teenager's age in the roster builder?

Add age: 15 (or age: 15 summer) to that person's row. The search then treats the limits above as hard rules, and any age under 18 also marks the person as someone who should not be alone on shift. Ages under 14 are refused.

whose-availability-is-worth-widening.htm.text:
← Shift roster builder

Whose availability is worth asking to widen?

When shifts stay open, the instinct is to ask whoever works the most. The better question is whose limit is actually in the way. We tested every person on one cafe roster: free them up to work any time, then separately raise their weekly cap to 40 hours, and rebuild the week each time.

Open the free roster builder

The experiment

The roster builder's built-in invented example: a seven-person cafe, 32 shifts, 235 hours to cover, a 10-hour rest gap. It starts with 3 shifts open, 216 hours covered and $3,622 payroll. For each person we changed one thing and rebuilt, leaving everything else as it was.

PersonFree at any timeWeekly cap raised to 40 h
OpenHoursPayrollOpenHoursPayroll
Ana3216$3,6223216$3,622
Ben3214$3,5942224$3,750
Cleo1227$3,7773216$3,622
Dev3211$3,5253216$3,622
Eli2219$3,6473216$3,622
Fay3211$3,5272224$3,746
Gus3216$3,6223216$3,622

What it shows

Only a few changes matter. Freeing Cleo, who is limited to evenings on weekdays, closes two of the three open shifts and lifts coverage to 227 hours. Raising the cap for Ben or Fay, who sit below 40 hours, closes one open shift each. Ana and Gus, the two people with the widest availability, change nothing either way: they were never the bottleneck. And freeing Ben, Dev or Fay slightly lowers the hours covered, because the search is a heuristic and a looser rule does not always find a bigger answer. This is one invented example, not a benchmark, and your own constraints decide who the right person is.

Test your own team

How to do it by hand

1. Start from the open shifts

List the shifts you could not fill and the reason each fails: nobody available, hour cap, or rest gap.

2. Ask the person whose limit is the reason

If the reason is an hour cap, ask the people near their cap. If it is availability, ask whoever is free just outside the shift.

3. Rebuild before you ask

Confirm that the change would fill the shift without creating overtime or breaking a rest gap, so the ask is specific.

Questions

Whose availability should I ask a team member to widen?

Rebuild the week once per person with that person free at any time, and compare open shifts. The person whose change closes the most open shifts is the one to ask. Often it is not the person with the most hours already; it is the one whose current availability misses the shifts nobody else can take. The roster builder shows which shifts stay open and why, which points at who to ask.

Is it worth asking someone to work more hours or more days?

Check whether the cap is what blocks the open shifts. In the example, raising the weekly limit for the two people sitting at their cap closed one open shift each, while raising it for people with room to spare changed nothing. Try the change in the tool before you ask.
